texts.title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.6-10.8: happiness and the life of the mind as a divine life
texts.source: Laur. Plut. 81.11 fol. 121v-124v (Teca Digitale, 10th c.) and Paris gr. 1854 fol. 175r-177v (Gallica, 12th c.) + Bywater Greek (Perseus) + H. Rackham English (Perseus)
texts.description: Aristotle's argument that the highest happiness is the activity of contemplation, a life 'higher than the human level' lived by the divine element in us: 'we ought so far as possible to achieve immortality' (1177b33). Shown on the oldest manuscript, Laur. Plut. 81.11 (10th c.), with its missing text supplied from Paris gr. 1854.

texts.title: Aristotle, Metaphysics 12.6-10 (Lambda): the unmoved mover and the life of god
texts.source: Paris gr. 1853 fol. 293r-296v (Gallica, 10th c.) + Ross Greek (Perseus) + W. D. Ross English (1928, MIT Internet Classics Archive)
texts.description: Aristotle's account of the first principle: an eternal, unmoved substance whose activity is thought thinking itself; 'the actuality of thought is life, and God is that actuality' (1072b). Shown on Paris gr. 1853, a 10th-century manuscript.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 4.184-185: Mount Atlas and the Atlantes
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (Herodotus A, 10th c.) fol. 193r-193v via Teca digitale BML + Godley's Greek (Perseus) + Macaulay's English (1890, Project Gutenberg)
texts.description: Herodotus on Mount Atlas, 'the pillar of heaven', and the Atlantes of Libya who eat no living thing and never dream (Histories 4.184-185), on the 10th-century manuscript Laur. Plut. 70.3, fol. 193r-193v.

texts.title: Diodorus of Sicily, Library 3.53-61: the Amazons of Libya and the myths of the Atlantians
texts.source: Vat. gr. 130 via DigiVatLib + Vogel's Greek (Perseus) + Oldfather's English (Loeb 1935, LacusCurtius)
texts.description: Diodorus on the Amazons of western Libya who conquered the Atlantians, and the Atlantians' own myths of Uranus, Atlas and the birth of the gods (Library 3.53-61), on Vat. gr. 130.

texts.title: Strabo, Geography 2.3.6: Posidonius on Plato's Atlantis
texts.source: Paris, BnF, grec 1397 (Strabo A) fol. 58r via Gallica (BnF) + Meineke's Greek (Perseus) + Hamilton and Falconer's English (1854-1857, Perseus)
texts.description: Strabo reports that Posidonius rightly cited Plato's view that the story of the island of Atlantis, told to Solon by the Egyptian priests, may not be a fiction (Geography 2.3.6), on Paris gr. 1397, fol. 58r.

texts.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 2.205: lands taken by the sea, 'if we believe Plato' in the Atlantic
texts.source: Leiden, UB, VLF 4 (Pliny A, 8th c.) fol. 4v-5r + Mayhoff's Latin (Perseus) + Bostock and Riley's English (1855, Perseus)
texts.description: Pliny the Elder on lands swallowed by the sea, first of all, 'if we believe Plato', a vast space where the Atlantic now is (Natural History 2.205), on the 8th-century manuscript Leiden VLF 4, fol. 4v-5r.

texts.title: Aelian, Varia Historia 3.18: Theopompus' tale of Midas and Silenus, the continent beyond Ocean and Meropis

texts.description: Aelian's summary of Theopompus' story told by Silenus to Midas: a vast continent beyond the Ocean, the cities Eusebes and Machimos, an invasion that turned back at the Hyperboreans, and the Meropes (Varia Historia 3.18), on Paris suppl. gr. 352.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Prologue (obverse, columns i-v)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: The prologue of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), in which Hammurabi names the gods who called him to rule and the cities he cared for, shown column by column on the Louvre stele.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 1-65 (obverse, columns v-xvi)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 1-65 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): false accusation and witnesses, judges, theft and receiving, kidnapping, runaway slaves, burglary and robbery, the fiefs of soldiers and tax-gatherers, fields, gardens, irrigation, and the leasing of orchards. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 100-149 (reverse, columns i-ix)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 100-149 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): merchants and their agents, wine-sellers, debt, pledges and deposits, slander, adultery, marriage, the wives of captives, divorce and the sick wife. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 150-199 (reverse, columns ix-xvii)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 150-199 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): gifts to wives, debts of husband and wife, incest, betrothal and the marriage settlement, dowries, inheritance, children of slave women, priestesses' shares, adoption, and bodily injury. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 200-249 (reverse, columns xvii-xxi)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 200-249 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): bodily injury and its payments, physicians, veterinary surgeons, branders, builders, boatmen, and hired oxen. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 250-282 (reverse, columns xxi-xxiii)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 250-282 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): the goring ox, the hire of oxen, farm hands and herdsmen, theft of farm implements, wages of labourers and craftsmen, hire of boats, and the sale of slaves. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Epilogue (reverse, columns xxiv-xxviii)

texts.title: Tacitus, Annals 15.44: Nero, the fire of Rome and the Christians

texts.description: Tacitus' account of Nero blaming the Christians for the fire of Rome in 64 AD, with the earliest Roman mention of Christ's execution under Pontius Pilate, shown on the 11th-century manuscript that alone preserves this part of the Annals.

texts.title: Suetonius, Claudius 25.4: the Jews expelled from Rome 'at the instigation of Chrestus'
texts.date_approx: c. 121 AD (composition); 11th c. (Cod. Guelf. 268 Gud. lat.)
texts.source: Wolfenbuettel, HAB, Cod. Guelf. 268 Gud. lat., fol. 109v-110r (Wolfenbuetteler Digitale Bibliothek) + Ihm's Latin (Perseus) + Rolfe's English (LacusCurtius)
texts.description: Suetonius' one-sentence notice that Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were rioting 'at the instigation of Chrestus', shown on an 11th-century manuscript page.

texts.title: Suetonius, Nero 16.2: 'punishment was inflicted on the Christians'
texts.date_approx: c. 121 AD (composition); 11th c. (Cod. Guelf. 268 Gud. lat.)
texts.source: Wolfenbuettel, HAB, Cod. Guelf. 268 Gud. lat., fol. 121r (Wolfenbuetteler Digitale Bibliothek) + Ihm's Latin (Perseus) + Rolfe's English (LacusCurtius)
texts.description: Suetonius lists the punishment of the Christians, 'a class of men given to a new and mischievous superstition', among Nero's measures, shown on an 11th-century manuscript page.

texts.title: Gilgameš and Ḫuwawa (Version A)
texts.source: CDLI photographs and transliterations of Old Babylonian tablets + ETCSL 1.8.1.5 English translation (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
texts.description: The Sumerian poem of Gilgameš and Enkidu's journey to the cedar mountain to kill the guardian Ḫuwawa, on the Old Babylonian tablets that carry it.

texts.title: Sumerian King List: the Weld-Blundell Prism (WB 444)
texts.date_approx: c. 1800 BCE (prism, reign of Sin-magir of Isin or soon after)
texts.source: Ashmolean Museum AN1923.444 photograph via CDLI (P384786) + CDLI transliteration of the prism + ETCSL 2.1.1 English translation (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)
texts.description: The Sumerian King List on the Weld-Blundell Prism (Ashmolean Museum, c. 1800 BCE), all four faces: the kings before the Flood, the Flood, and the dynasties after it down to Isin.

texts.title: The Babylonian Theodicy (dialogue of the sufferer and his friend)
texts.date_approx: composed c. 1000 BCE; tablets 7th-2nd c. BCE
texts.source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L II.1, Theodicy, SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
texts.description: The Babylonian Theodicy, dialogue: 258 of 288 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (10 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
